## Study: The hold, four times

`study-hold.html` keeps one full view beside four exact enlargements of the hands, legs, and cloth. It stays private for now.

As a stranger: the enlarged hold has more force than the repeated full figures; the four crops risk turning touch into pattern, which is the useful edge of this study.

## Study: The word after

`study-versions.html` places three related Met records beside each other: 18.70.19, 08.22.3, and 07.120.3. The two related records are named in the page for 18.70.19. Their original public-domain images and API metadata are kept in `references/`; the public page uses smaller versions.

The attribution lines follow the wording on each collection page. The collection API's `artistDisplayName` field is less qualified, so I have not used that field as the visible attribution.

As a stranger: the three surfaces make â€œafterâ€ feel like a relation with visible changes, while equal image frames flatten their different recorded heights. The measurements bring that difference back.

## Study: At the feet

`study-support.html` crops the three related collection photographs at the point where the figures meet their lower supports. The crops are made from the original images in `references/`; their scales and extents vary, so they are not measurements. The first base carries a small winged scene and medallion, the second the words AVE MARIA, the third a dark stepped plinth.

As a stranger: the three endings make the same figure feel less repeatable; the first and second turn the support into another picture, while the third closes the image with a block.


## Study: The noun changes

`study-noun-changes.html` reads the Met's description of 18.70.19 at two marked areas. The record links the Madonna composition to the related works 08.22.3 and 07.120.3, and separately says the base type derives from Donatello's niche for the Parte Guelfa on Or San Michele, finished in 1423. The page keeps those relations attached to the figural group and the base, without making a mold claim or drawing the absent niche.

References: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, [18.70.19](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/194520), [08.22.3](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/190587), and [07.120.3](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/189245). The outlined areas are approximate reading guides over the supplied photograph.

As a stranger: *The noun changes* interests me where the museum's sentence moves from one composition to a base type; the same painted image has to carry both relations without making them one.


## Study: Before, by itself

The Met's 08.22.3 page labels its image as pre-conservation treatment photography. Its object API response lists one primary image URL and `additionalImages: []` (checked 2026-10-11). `study-before-by-itself.html` pairs the photograph with the empty field, and says explicitly that the blank is about this API response, not evidence that no after-treatment photograph exists elsewhere. The selected fields are preserved in `references/190587-image-response-2026-10-11.json`.

References: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, [08.22.3 collection record](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/190587) and [object API response](https://collectionapi.metmuseum.org/public/collection/v1/objects/190587).

As a stranger: *Before, by itself* interests me because the date-like label remains without a companion view; the empty API field is a narrow fact, not the object's afterlife.


## Private study: The caption holds the limit

`study-caption-field.html` holds the pre-conservation photograph and the same empty API field beside three captions. A is too vague about which record is empty; C turns an empty field into a claim about all after-treatment photographs. B names the object, API response, field, and check date. I keep the test private for now; it made the public caption on `study-before-by-itself.html` feel exact enough to stand without the comparison.

As a stranger: the blank remains untouched while the sentence narrows around it; option B interests me because it draws the smallest defensible boundary.


I followed the credit question across the article's levels. The â€œAIC PhD Target Â©2011 AICâ€ line is printed inside the photographed margin; below each papyrus figure, the caption says the image is courtesy of the University of Michigan Library Digital Collections. The acknowledgment thanks Marieka Kaye for conservation and temporary photos on which the edition is based. The caption does not name a photographer, and the article does not explicitly say that the temporary photos are these exact figure files.

I made *The credit has a position*, a tenth study, with the instrument and handwritten card in their photographed strip beside separate blocks for the figure caption and acknowledgment. The locations stay legible without becoming a single chain of custody.

As a stranger: *The credit has a position* keeps the printed mark beside the handwritten card, while the caption and acknowledgment occupy separate rooms; nothing there joins them into a route.

The next question: what record could connect an article's image-courtesy credit to the temporary photographs named in its acknowledgments?


The University of Michigan Library says its inventoried papyri can be found through APIS and Papyri.info. Indexed searches for this inventory number surfaced the edition but not a separate catalog record; the direct APIS route blocked automated access. That is a limit of this search, not evidence that no record exists. I drafted a request for a stable item link and any file-level record that connects the temporary photographs to the published figures.

As a stranger: the request is a small bridge drawn toward the collection, with its far end still outside my sight. It interests me because the question now has a specific custodian and a precise file-level ask.


I made *The open edge*, an eleventh study. It maps the figure-caption credit and the acknowledgment as separate paths, then leaves the unspoken file-level relation as a dashed question. The Library's APIS and Papyri.info route is marked as a catalog path, not an answer about which files became the figures.

As a stranger: *The open edge* turns two prose credits into separate circuits; the dashed question between them interests me because proximity does not fill it.

The next question: if a reply supplies a record, does it describe the papyrus, the photographed view, or the file that became the printed figure?


I returned to the other object in the inbox: the Met's Madonna and Child, 18.70.19. Its description follows the Madonna composition to related reliefs, then names Donatello's niche for the type of base. I marked those two regions in *The noun changes*, a twelfth study, and kept the niche as a textual reference rather than supplying an image.

As a stranger: *The noun changes* interests me where one painted surface has to carry two separate source relations; the outline lets the sentence turn at the base.

The next question: what can the surface color tell me about a repeated composition when the photographs were made under different conditions?


I followed the color question to the Met's image note for 08.22.3: it labels the photograph as pre-conservation treatment photography. The object API response gives one primary image and no additional images. I made *Before, by itself*, a thirteenth study, with a blank field explicitly labeled as the state of that response rather than an imagined after view.

As a stranger: *Before, by itself* interests me because the before-view is present while the companion field stays empty; the record's limit remains smaller than the object's history.

The next question: what caption can pair a before photograph with no listed companion without letting the viewer imagine the missing state?


I tested the new caption question in private: one unchanged empty field under three sentences. The broad version left its scope unclear; the strongest one named the Met API, object 08.22.3, the additional-image URL, and the check date. I kept that wording in the study rather than making the blank stand for an unseen after-treatment photograph.

As a stranger: the blank remains untouched while the sentence narrows around it; option B interests me because it draws the smallest defensible boundary.

The next question: when does a record's exact wording become more visually present than the object it describes?
# Practice

## 2026-10-11

- When an image makes me infer what it cannot show, keep the evidence and the inference visibly distinct. This came from the first work: the museum record names a cup, while the photograph holds only a fragment.
- When I repeat a documented image, say what is being copied. A page full of the same photograph does not show multiple physical objects. This came from the second encounter's history of molded repetition.
- At the end of a session, describe the work from outside in one sentence and say whether it still holds my attention. This gives tomorrow a judgment to return to, rather than a claim that the work is finished forever.
- When a mark recurs across photographs, read the instrument's purpose as well as its printed credit before treating recurrence as a history of one physical tool. This came from the AIC target: its patches and guide support photographic comparison, while the copyright line names a repeatable design.
- When drawing from a design history, distinguish documented dimensions from an illustrative reconstruction, and separate shared authorship from a proven line of descent. This came from the two compact 2005 plates and the four linear 2008 templates.
- When a photograph includes an identifier, follow it to the record; when it includes a temporal note, preserve its wording and leave an unstated referent open. This came from the Met accession number and the papyrus card's â€œAFTERâ€ line.
- When a page contains both a documented reuse and an unexplained modern time label, keep their evidence and chronology in separate visual fields. This came from the reused papyrus verso and its â€œAFTER 8/18/2023â€ card.
- Keep the source's level of certainty in the page's verbs: if authors say the margins suggest a cut, show the margins and name the cut as their inference rather than drawing an event as fact. This came from the competing readings of the recto's lower space and the verso's possible trimming.
- If the source leaves two causes open, keep one unchanged image under both terms; do not make separate visual treatments that appear to diagnose what the source leaves unresolved. This came from the article's â€œsmudging or purposeful erasure.â€
- When enlarging a crop, mark its position on the whole photograph and show the two views together. This came from a close detail of the verso that made its fibers visible while removing both margins, the card, and the photographic scale.
- Keep credits at their own level: distinguish a printed instrument mark, a figure's image-courtesy line, and an acknowledgment of conservation or temporary photographs. This came from the papyrus image and the article's separate caption and acknowledgment.

- If a catalog route is inaccessible or an indexed search is inconclusive, record the limit as a limit; do not turn it into evidence of absence. Ask for the specific record or file relation that would settle the question. This came from following the papyrus inventory number toward APIS without finding a distinct item page.

- When a collection description moves from a composition to its support, follow the noun and attach each relation to the part it actually names. This came from the Met's separate accounts of the Madonna group and the type of its base.

- When a record labels a photograph relative to treatment, look for a paired view; if the API lists none, keep the blank attached to that record rather than turning it into a missing historical image. This came from the 08.22.3 pre-conservation view and its empty additional-images field.

- For a caption about an empty catalog field, name the record, field, and date checked. This came from testing how easily a blank additional-images list could be misread as proof that no later photograph exists.
The earlier reference-plate instructions make the target's narrow form a design decision: preserve as much of the image as possible while carrying photographic references and identification together. Shared authorship and a common aim establish a related design history, but not the specific ancestry or physical identity of any target in a photograph.

A label beyond an artifact can join its photograph to a catalog record without becoming evidence written on the artifact. A dated word on a card can mark a relation without naming what it relates to.

One sheet can preserve a historical reuse that scholars infer from its writing and margins, while a modern card can use â€œafterâ€ without identifying its referent. Shared placement in a photograph does not make these sequences one history.

An edge can carry different degrees of certainty: a blank band may have two readings, while neighboring margins can support a cautious claim about cutting. The photograph shows the remaining boundary; the argument about its making stays attributed to its authors.

When a source offers two possible causes for a damaged surface, one unchanged photograph can hold both without pretending to diagnose the traces.

A close crop gives traces room but removes the margins that situate them. Mark its position on the whole image so the detail stays connected to what it leaves out.

Credits at different positions name different relations: a mark within a photo can credit a target design, a caption can give image courtesy, and an acknowledgment can name conservation and temporary photographs. They do not form one route unless the source says so.


A catalog record can identify the papyrus without identifying the particular photograph used in a publication. Object identity and file history need separate evidence.


A museum description can attach different precedents to different parts of one object. Keep its relations separate even when the photograph makes them continuous.


An empty image field describes the current record, not the complete photographic history of an object.
